Eskom Lights Out!

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Christmas lights may have stayed on, but cash strapped and poorly serviced Eskom may not be able to abate this energy crisis. Is there any light at the end of a very dark tunnel?

Unique Selling Point:
Eskom is in a death spiral and has the power to break the South African economy. There are solutions that could help change this picture of gloom, but will the political pre-election climate allow any of these solutions to become a reality, or is there too much at stake for government to lose?

Summary:
Cash strapped power utility Eskom has been struggling with its balance sheet for years. State Capture, corruption, poor quality coal, unscheduled maintenance, design flaws at Medupe and Kusile are just some of the issues causing its spiraling debt, now sitting at R420Bn. That debt is expected to rise by an additional R200Bn, comprising of loan repayments and for the completion of Kusile and Medupe Power Stations, which will leave it approximately R600Bn in the red this year. Eskom requested a R100Bn bail out from government, but experts say, this is an unsustainable business model that will eventually collapse. Will Eskom be able to dig itself out of this dark hole and shed some light on the nation? Carte Blanche finds out.

Further information:
Minister of Public Enterprises Pravin Gordhan blames load shedding on the fact that Eskom's power stations have not been maintained. A lot of these maintenance issues arose as a result of money being spent on dubious State Capture ventures. The 2 billion Rand that was reserved for maintenance for 2015/2016 was rather spent on 1.5 Billion rand paid to McKinsey and Trillian and another 658 million rand that was paid as a repayment to the Gupta's mining company Tegeta Resources and Exploration for coal, additionally hundreds of millions of rands were paid to Tegeta for coal that was never delivered.

Energy Analyst, Chris Yelland, believes that we can't continue blaming state capture for all of Eskom's woes and there is no way of turning back the clock. He says that Eskom's burgeoning debt of 600 Billion rand, leaves it with no business resilience and that it is shackled by a political and ideological impasse. People's salaries are three times more than what they should be, and labour is holding Eskom to ransom. The prospect of privatization is not on the cards as it is ideologically at loggerheads with the current political climate. This means that it is unsustainable for Eskom to continue the way it is, borrowing money to pay it's debt and it has no way of creating a business model in its current state that will change the outcome. Eskom is also at the mercy of NERSA that sets the tariffs, and has not approved Eskom's request of a 15% electricity hike.

COO of Eskom, Jan Oberholzer says the impact of the Medupe and Kusile outages in December 2018 are not negligible. We speak to him about the operational setbacks and strategies to correct some of the problems going forward for 2019 and the future.

We speak to Zwelinzima Vavi of SAFTU, who was very critical of Eskom Chairman Jabu Mabuza's comment “All South African's need to take responsibility for Eskom's loadshedding”. He also addresses the pressing labour issues which continually threaten to destabilise the power utility.


Business big and small are threatened by the prospect of continued load shedding predicted to last throughout the first half of 2019, how is this going to affect the overall South African Economy and can we withstand the loss? What will it ultimately cost South Africa? If Eskom's bailout means more borrowing in the future, how will it impact business and the Economy? Alan Mukoki CEO of SA Chamber of Commerce and Industry addresses these issues.

Grove Steyn is an energy economist that will speak to possible solutions going forward. The solutions aren't easy and have to have a multi-faceted approach, some of which have not been too much in the public domain, but would need Eskom and government to commit to decarbonisation, which does not fit the government's overall political agenda, especially pre-elections.

There is a report and a plan that is being put together that will probably only be announced at SONA, but again this report may just pander to pre-election rhetoric and not have the hard solutions that would be necessary to take SA energy crisis going forward.

Eskom has the power to destabilise the South African economy to such an extent that they could find themselves in front of the IMF or World Bank, and ultimately we could see SA facing economic breakdown to the extent of Greece, Argentina and Portugual. What will it take to stop the death spiral of Eskom?

Press Release:


Ballooning debt and operational inefficiency is plaguing South Africa’s energy monopoly Eskom. The consequences of not tackling the utilities problems are catastrophic. Could the global shift towards energy transition form part of the solution?


Script:


Montage electricity:
family watching TV, cooking and then the lights go off.

Title: Stage two load shedding - 2018

Time lapse shot transition into link…

LINK: You may have experienced the festive season with the lights on, but that doesn’t mean that Eskom’s energy crisis is over, with 480 billion rand in the red, will the power utility be able to keep the lights on, in the year ahead?

Yelland: the line between load shedding and not load shedding is very thin indeed.

Vavi: Load shedding represents a catastrophe for SA economy, it’s a disaster.

VO: According to Energy Analyst, Chris Yelland the cost to the economy of electricity not delivered to the grid is estimated at R75 per kilowatt hour.

Yelland: It works out to 2 billion rand per day cost to the economy of stage 2 load shedding [02:02:47.23] for 13 hours a day.

VO: Zwelinzima Vavi, General Secretary, of the South African Federation of Trade Unions, is concerned about the real impact on the country.

Vavi: Who can be excited about investing in an economy which has such an unpredictable source of energy.

Yelland: if eskom fails dramatically, it has the potential to dim the lights in SA and Eskom's management is gripped with that goal to avoid load shedding at all costs.

VO: Even though the state-owned power utility’s operational problems will take years to rectify, in an attempt to avert the crisis, in December, Minister of Public Enterprises, Pravin Gordhan ordered Eskom management and staff to cancel their holidays and work on priority maintenance.

Chartered accountant and analyst Khaya Sithole, regularly studies Eskom’s financial reports.

Khaya: Over the christmas season a lot of the large users of power are off the grid so it’s difficult for us to assess using that particular period and establish that Eskom is now in a position to ensure that the lights can be kept on.

VO: So now, with South Africa back at work in full swing we’ll soon know how successful this maintenance really was. The prospect of further load shedding has South Africans on edge, particularly those living in townships and rural areas, as criminals take advantage of darkness for cover.

Vavi: We must look at the issue of eskom in its totality as an impact, its a social crisis making everything that is bad worse.

Yelland: Eskom currently has debt of 480 billion rand, the most significant part is debt caused by the construction and financing of Madupe and Kusile which in my estimation amounts to between 250 to 300 billion rand

VO: Eskom’s debt is expected to rise to 600 Billion Rand within 4 years. And the utility’s financial woes are not helped by the 30 billion rand of outstanding bills owed by Municipalities.

LINK: Poor maintenance, state capture, bad governance, lack of coal supplies, insufficient planning, and the overly inflated costs of building kusile and medupe, these are just some of problems that Eskom is faced with, but what is really to blame for the rot at the utility?

Vavi: The real story is that way back in 1997 1998 eskom warned our government, you have to invest in more generation capacity, you have to renew the infrastructure and they didn’t do it.It will take you 10 years before you hit the real crisis of load shedding. Indeed in 2008 the crisis began. the former president Jacob Zuma. He wasted no time to make that already bad situation even worse.

VO: Some experts believe that we can't continue blaming state capture for all of Eskom's ills, but it was the buzzword for 2018.

Khaya: I think when you look at the executives that have fired primarily at the beginning of last year that was really part of the governance and what came out to the public was the fact that there was a rot within the boardroom of eskom.

Sound up Pravin: All of you in the top management and the board of Eskom were part of this conspiracy.

VO: These executives continued to deny any wrongdoing.//

And again in December, in order to cut costs, more executives were slashed. Yet Eskom still has 207 more senior managers than it did 17 years ago.

LINK: Eskom pays some of the highest salaries across all state owned entities, however it is also over staffed, but can the utility afford to lay off people without the labour movement bringing the country to its knees?

Vavi: Are you saying we must agree that 2 thirds of workers must be thrown into the streets and that labour must agree to cut 2 thirds of their salary and in order to be patriotic and to pay so dearly with our very lives.

LINK: Eskom supplies 95% of South Africa's electricity, meaning that it has a centralized monopoly in the energy sector, however its business model has become unsustainable, facing what is called a utility death or debt spiral.

Khaya: In an environment where you cannot generate sufficient additional revenue, whatever revenue you're generating is being eaten away by the interest cost but if you then need to actually borrow more money your debt burden keeps ballooning so its a debt spiral that eskom finds itself in.

VO: Eskom is also at the mercy of the National Energy Regulator which sets the tariffs, and has not approved Eskom's request of a 15% electricity hike.

Yelland: Simply putting up prices causes people to use less of its product, forcing eskom to put up its prices again and people use less again and you get into the spiral known as the utility death spiral.

VO: Utilities are facing this death spiral all around the world and have had to look at alternative solutions. Currently Eskom is asking government for a 100 billion rand bailout.

Khaya: You could shift some liabilities onto the national treasury balance sheet The consequence is that debt to GDP ratio will incrementally increase.


Yelland: But government has made it clear that this 100 billion rand bailout or transferring debt from eskom to treasury is not on.

Khaya: Eskom is a unique entity in that eskom could shut the country down over night not just by switching off the lights but by simply making us bankrupt.

VO: So in order for the utility to break the cycle, it has to find solutions outside its current business model. Davin Chown, Chairperson of the South African Photovoltaic Industry Association, has been involved in the renewable energy sector since 2001 and points to the fact that globally there is a move towards an energy transition.

Davin: The energy transition is something that says we've got a carbon problem we've got to deal with, we've developed a power system around the world that is highly centralized, very polluting and is not flexible and adaptive to the needs of a modern economy whichever part of the globe you're in.

VO: And the draft Integrated Resource Plan outlined by government does reflect this shift.

Davin: SA has got a very ambitious plan to participate in the energy transition. That means a mix of renewables, gas and a bit of coal. It means a decentralized energy system and it means we are going to refurbish the grid and we're going to make the delivery of power throughout our grid, a lot more responsive and cheaper for SA.

Vavi: We as the unions have embraced the need to move us towards a cleaner environment, carbon based economies cannot be sustained, we need to move but then we dont want that to be done by the private sectors we want to be done by governments that care about all of the issues that we are raising.

VO: The global move towards decarbonization has opened up the opportunity for countries to get big funding that will assist their change to cleaner power.

Davin: If eskom says we are going to change the way we procure our power and from whom we do it and we want to work in partnership to develop renewable energy asset, then funds will be accessed but it won’t be accessed to bail eskom out of its current situation.

Vavi: All I’m saying is the situation where you allow people to have (LIGHTS GO OUT) Load shedding, load shedding electricity has just gone, we must leave this life you are a small firm, you don’t have a generator to kick in, what happens? workers get sent home.

VO: And so were we..

visuals of us going down dark stairs

LINK: Can you guys see me? There we go. So even the Carte Blanche team wasn't exempt when the lights went out during an interview. Load shedding affects everyone from factories, businesses and households

VO: Eskom were unavailable for an interview, but in their most recent media statement they expressed a commitment to "improving operational efficiencies and reducing costs to improve profitability”. Last year the President appointed a task team to consider Eskom’s options and crucially its runaway debt.

Yelland: Putting up prices, cutting costs, refinancing its debt, taking on strategic equity partners, increasing public participation in the business, all of these are possible options. Some of them are politically acceptable, some are very difficult.

LINK: The task teams challenge is to provide solutions by the end of January, but who knows if their answers will stop South Africa's lights from going out?

Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 13 January 2019 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 31 January 2019 Press Release: Ballooning debt and operational inefficiency is plaguing South Africa’s energy monopoly Eskom. The consequences of not tackling the utilities problems are catastrophic. Could the global shift towards energy transition form part of the solution? Script: Montage electricity: family watching TV, cooking and then the lights go off. Title: Stage two load shedding - 2018 Time lapse shot transition into link… LINK: You may have experienced the festive season with the lights on, but that doesn’t mean that Eskom’s energy crisis is over, with 480 billion rand in the red, will the power utility be able to keep the lights on, in the year ahead? Yelland: the line between load shedding and not load shedding is very thin indeed. Vavi: Load shedding represents a catastrophe for SA economy, it’s a disaster. VO: According to Energy Analyst, Chris Yelland the cost to the economy of electricity not delivered to the grid is estimated at R75 per kilowatt hour. Yelland: It works out to 2 billion rand per day cost to the economy of stage 2 load shedding [02:02:47.23] for 13 hours a day. VO: Zwelinzima Vavi, General Secretary, of the South African Federation of Trade Unions, is concerned about the real impact on the country. Vavi: Who can be excited about investing in an economy which has such an unpredictable source of energy. Yelland: if eskom fails dramatically, it has the potential to dim the lights in SA and Eskom's management is gripped with that goal to avoid load shedding at all costs. VO: Even though the state-owned power utility’s operational problems will take years to rectify, in an attempt to avert the crisis, in December, Minister of Public Enterprises, Pravin Gordhan ordered Eskom management and staff to cancel their holidays and work on priority maintenance. Chartered accountant and analyst Khaya Sithole, regularly studies Eskom’s financial reports. Khaya: Over the christmas season a lot of the large users of power are off the grid so it’s difficult for us to assess using that particular period and establish that Eskom is now in a position to ensure that the lights can be kept on. VO: So now, with South Africa back at work in full swing we’ll soon know how successful this maintenance really was. The prospect of further load shedding has South Africans on edge, particularly those living in townships and rural areas, as criminals take advantage of darkness for cover. Vavi: We must look at the issue of eskom in its totality as an impact, its a social crisis making everything that is bad worse. Yelland: Eskom currently has debt of 480 billion rand, the most significant part is debt caused by the construction and financing of Madupe and Kusile which in my estimation amounts to between 250 to 300 billion rand VO: Eskom’s debt is expected to rise to 600 Billion Rand within 4 years. And the utility’s financial woes are not helped by the 30 billion rand of outstanding bills owed by Municipalities. LINK: Poor maintenance, state capture, bad governance, lack of coal supplies, insufficient planning, and the overly inflated costs of building kusile and medupe, these are just some of problems that Eskom is faced with, but what is really to blame for the rot at the utility? Vavi: The real story is that way back in 1997 1998 eskom warned our government, you have to invest in more generation capacity, you have to renew the infrastructure and they didn’t do it.It will take you 10 years before you hit the real crisis of load shedding. Indeed in 2008 the crisis began. the former president Jacob Zuma. He wasted no time to make that already bad situation even worse. VO: Some experts believe that we can't continue blaming state capture for all of Eskom's ills, but it was the buzzword for 2018. Khaya: I think when you look at the executives that have fired primarily at the beginning of last year that was really part of the governance and what came out to the public was the fact that there was a rot within the boardroom of eskom. Sound up Pravin: All of you in the top management and the board of Eskom were part of this conspiracy. VO: These executives continued to deny any wrongdoing.// And again in December, in order to cut costs, more executives were slashed. Yet Eskom still has 207 more senior managers than it did 17 years ago. LINK: Eskom pays some of the highest salaries across all state owned entities, however it is also over staffed, but can the utility afford to lay off people without the labour movement bringing the country to its knees? Vavi: Are you saying we must agree that 2 thirds of workers must be thrown into the streets and that labour must agree to cut 2 thirds of their salary and in order to be patriotic and to pay so dearly with our very lives. LINK: Eskom supplies 95% of South Africa's electricity, meaning that it has a centralized monopoly in the energy sector, however its business model has become unsustainable, facing what is called a utility death or debt spiral. Khaya: In an environment where you cannot generate sufficient additional revenue, whatever revenue you're generating is being eaten away by the interest cost but if you then need to actually borrow more money your debt burden keeps ballooning so its a debt spiral that eskom finds itself in. VO: Eskom is also at the mercy of the National Energy Regulator which sets the tariffs, and has not approved Eskom's request of a 15% electricity hike. Yelland: Simply putting up prices causes people to use less of its product, forcing eskom to put up its prices again and people use less again and you get into the spiral known as the utility death spiral. VO: Utilities are facing this death spiral all around the world and have had to look at alternative solutions. Currently Eskom is asking government for a 100 billion rand bailout. Khaya: You could shift some liabilities onto the national treasury balance sheet The consequence is that debt to GDP ratio will incrementally increase. Yelland: But government has made it clear that this 100 billion rand bailout or transferring debt from eskom to treasury is not on. Khaya: Eskom is a unique entity in that eskom could shut the country down over night not just by switching off the lights but by simply making us bankrupt. VO: So in order for the utility to break the cycle, it has to find solutions outside its current business model. Davin Chown, Chairperson of the South African Photovoltaic Industry Association, has been involved in the renewable energy sector since 2001 and points to the fact that globally there is a move towards an energy transition. Davin: The energy transition is something that says we've got a carbon problem we've got to deal with, we've developed a power system around the world that is highly centralized, very polluting and is not flexible and adaptive to the needs of a modern economy whichever part of the globe you're in. VO: And the draft Integrated Resource Plan outlined by government does reflect this shift. Davin: SA has got a very ambitious plan to participate in the energy transition. That means a mix of renewables, gas and a bit of coal. It means a decentralized energy system and it means we are going to refurbish the grid and we're going to make the delivery of power throughout our grid, a lot more responsive and cheaper for SA. Vavi: We as the unions have embraced the need to move us towards a cleaner environment, carbon based economies cannot be sustained, we need to move but then we dont want that to be done by the private sectors we want to be done by governments that care about all of the issues that we are raising. VO: The global move towards decarbonization has opened up the opportunity for countries to get big funding that will assist their change to cleaner power. Davin: If eskom says we are going to change the way we procure our power and from whom we do it and we want to work in partnership to develop renewable energy asset, then funds will be accessed but it won’t be accessed to bail eskom out of its current situation. Vavi: All I’m saying is the situation where you allow people to have (LIGHTS GO OUT) Load shedding, load shedding electricity has just gone, we must leave this life you are a small firm, you don’t have a generator to kick in, what happens? workers get sent home. VO: And so were we.. visuals of us going down dark stairs LINK: Can you guys see me? There we go. So even the Carte Blanche team wasn't exempt when the lights went out during an interview. Load shedding affects everyone from factories, businesses and households VO: Eskom were unavailable for an interview, but in their most recent media statement they expressed a commitment to "improving operational efficiencies and reducing costs to improve profitability”. Last year the President appointed a task team to consider Eskom’s options and crucially its runaway debt. Yelland: Putting up prices, cutting costs, refinancing its debt, taking on strategic equity partners, increasing public participation in the business, all of these are possible options. Some of them are politically acceptable, some are very difficult. LINK: The task teams challenge is to provide solutions by the end of January, but who knows if their answers will stop South Africa's lights from going out?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Christmas lights may have stayed on, but cash strapped and poorly serviced Eskom may not be able to abate this energy crisis. Is there any light at the end of a very dark tunnel?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Eskom is in a death spiral and has the power to break the South African economy. There are solutions that could help change this picture of gloom, but will the political pre-election climate allow any of these solutions to become a reality, or is there too much at stake for government to lose?
metadata.Summary: Cash strapped power utility Eskom has been struggling with its balance sheet for years. State Capture, corruption, poor quality coal, unscheduled maintenance, design flaws at Medupe and Kusile are just some of the issues causing its spiraling debt, now sitting at R420Bn. That debt is expected to rise by an additional R200Bn, comprising of loan repayments and for the completion of Kusile and Medupe Power Stations, which will leave it approximately R600Bn in the red this year. Eskom requested a R100Bn bail out from government, but experts say, this is an unsustainable business model that will eventually collapse. Will Eskom be able to dig itself out of this dark hole and shed some light on the nation? Carte Blanche finds out.
metadata.Further information: Minister of Public Enterprises Pravin Gordhan blames load shedding on the fact that Eskom's power stations have not been maintained. A lot of these maintenance issues arose as a result of money being spent on dubious State Capture ventures. The 2 billion Rand that was reserved for maintenance for 2015/2016 was rather spent on 1.5 Billion rand paid to McKinsey and Trillian and another 658 million rand that was paid as a repayment to the Gupta's mining company Tegeta Resources and Exploration for coal, additionally hundreds of millions of rands were paid to Tegeta for coal that was never delivered. Energy Analyst, Chris Yelland, believes that we can't continue blaming state capture for all of Eskom's woes and there is no way of turning back the clock. He says that Eskom's burgeoning debt of 600 Billion rand, leaves it with no business resilience and that it is shackled by a political and ideological impasse. People's salaries are three times more than what they should be, and labour is holding Eskom to ransom. The prospect of privatization is not on the cards as it is ideologically at loggerheads with the current political climate. This means that it is unsustainable for Eskom to continue the way it is, borrowing money to pay it's debt and it has no way of creating a business model in its current state that will change the outcome. Eskom is also at the mercy of NERSA that sets the tariffs, and has not approved Eskom's request of a 15% electricity hike. COO of Eskom, Jan Oberholzer says the impact of the Medupe and Kusile outages in December 2018 are not negligible. We speak to him about the operational setbacks and strategies to correct some of the problems going forward for 2019 and the future. We speak to Zwelinzima Vavi of SAFTU, who was very critical of Eskom Chairman Jabu Mabuza's comment “All South African's need to take responsibility for Eskom's loadshedding”. He also addresses the pressing labour issues which continually threaten to destabilise the power utility. Business big and small are threatened by the prospect of continued load shedding predicted to last throughout the first half of 2019, how is this going to affect the overall South African Economy and can we withstand the loss? What will it ultimately cost South Africa? If Eskom's bailout means more borrowing in the future, how will it impact business and the Economy? Alan Mukoki CEO of SA Chamber of Commerce and Industry addresses these issues. Grove Steyn is an energy economist that will speak to possible solutions going forward. The solutions aren't easy and have to have a multi-faceted approach, some of which have not been too much in the public domain, but would need Eskom and government to commit to decarbonisation, which does not fit the government's overall political agenda, especially pre-elections. There is a report and a plan that is being put together that will probably only be announced at SONA, but again this report may just pander to pre-election rhetoric and not have the hard solutions that would be necessary to take SA energy crisis going forward. Eskom has the power to destabilise the South African economy to such an extent that they could find themselves in front of the IMF or World Bank, and ultimately we could see SA facing economic breakdown to the extent of Greece, Argentina and Portugual. What will it take to stop the death spiral of Eskom?
